pattern: ich · du · er / sie / es · wir · ihr · sie · Sie
explain: Personal pronouns stand for people and things: ich (I), du (you), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they). For one 'you', choose: du for friends, family and children, Sie for adults you don't know well, like a teacher or a neighbour. Polite Sie always has a capital S.
compare_en: English has one 'you'; German picks du (friendly), ihr (friendly, several people) or Sie (polite, one or more). sie can mean 'she' or 'they', and Sie means polite 'you': the verb ending helps you tell them apart.

pattern: verb stem + ending: ich -e · du -st · er / sie / es -t
explain: A German verb changes its ending to match the subject (who does it). Take the infinitive, e.g. wohnen, drop -en to get the stem wohn-, then add the ending: ich wohne, du wohnst, er wohnt. If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z, du only adds -t: du heißt. If it ends in -t or -d, add an extra e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
compare_en: English only adds -s for he, she and it (he lives). German gives almost every person its own ending, so the ending tells you who is doing it.

pattern: W-word + VERB + subject + …?
explain: W-questions ask for information. They start with a question word: wer? (who), wie? (how), wo? (where), woher? (where from), was? (what). The verb comes straight after it, in position 2, and then the subject. To ask someone's name, German uses wie: Wie heißt du?
compare_en: English often needs 'do' (Where do you live?). German never does: the verb itself stands in position 2: Wo wohnst du? Careful: wer means 'who', not 'where'.

pattern: ich bin · du bist · er / sie / es ist · wir sind · ihr seid · sie / Sie sind
explain: sein (to be) is the most important verb, and it is irregular, so learn its forms by heart. Use it to say who you are, where you are from, how old you are and what someone is like: Ich bin Priya. Ich bin 25 Jahre alt. For jobs, German uses no 'a': Jonas ist Student.
compare_en: Like 'to be', sein is irregular in English too (I am, you are, he is). But German drops the 'a' with jobs: Ich bin Student = I am a student.

pattern: wir -en · ihr -t · sie / Sie -en
explain: In the plural, wir, sie (they) and Sie (polite you) all use the infinitive form: wir wohnen, sie wohnen, Sie wohnen. Only ihr (you, several friends) is different: it takes -t, like er: ihr wohnt. After a stem ending in -t or -d, ihr adds -et: ihr arbeitet.
compare_en: In English, we, you and they share one form (we live, they live). German is the same for wir, sie and Sie, but ihr has its own -t ending: ihr wohnt.

pattern: VERB + subject + …?
explain: A yes/no question starts with the verb, and the subject comes right after it: Kommst du aus Indien? Wohnt Lena in Köln? The answer begins with ja (yes) or nein (no). When you speak, your voice goes up at the end.
compare_en: English adds do/does (Do you come from India?) or turns 'is' around (Is he married?). German just puts the verb first, for every verb: Kommst du …? Ist er …? There is no 'do'.

pattern: position 1 + VERB (position 2) + …
explain: In a German statement the verb with the ending always stands in position 2. Position 1 is one block: often the subject, but it can also be a word like hier or a phrase like in Berlin. A block can have several words: Lena und Jonas is one position. If something else is in position 1, the subject goes right after the verb.
compare_en: English keeps the subject before the verb: Here I live. German keeps the verb in position 2, even if the subject then comes after it: Hier wohne ich.

pattern: ich habe · du hast · er / sie / es hat · wir haben · ihr habt · sie / Sie haben
explain: haben means 'to have'. It is almost regular, but du and er/sie/es lose the b: du hast, er hat. Use it for family, things and time: Ich habe zwei Brüder. Hast du Zeit? Some feelings also use haben: Ich habe Hunger (I'm hungry), Ich habe Durst (I'm thirsty).
compare_en: haben works like 'have' (I have a brother). But where English says 'I am hungry', German says Ich habe Hunger, literally 'I have hunger'.

pattern: der / ein (masculine) · die / eine (feminine) · das / ein (neuter) · die (plural)
explain: Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). Use der/die/das (the) for something already known, and ein/eine (a) for something new: Das ist ein Hund. Der Hund ist klein. In the plural the article is always die, and there is no plural of ein. Learn every noun with its article.
compare_en: English has one 'the' and one 'a'. German has three genders, and they don't always follow meaning: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter.

pattern: mein / dein / sein / ihr + noun (endings like ein)
explain: Possessive words say whose something is: mein (my), dein (your), sein (his), ihr (her), unser (our), euer (your, several friends), ihr (their), Ihr (your, polite). They take the same endings as ein: mein Vater, meine Mutter, mein Kind, meine Eltern.
compare_en: As in English, the owner decides: Jonas → sein (his), Lena → ihr (her). But German also adds -e when the thing owned is feminine or plural: sein Bruder, seine Schwester.

pattern: subject + verb + den / einen + masculine noun (the object)
explain: The object is the person or thing the action is done to: Ich trinke einen Kaffee. It is in the accusative case. Good news: only masculine nouns change: der → den, ein → einen. Feminine (die, eine), neuter (das, ein) and plural stay the same. Verbs like haben, essen, trinken, nehmen and bestellen take an object.
compare_en: English shows this only with pronouns (he → him). German shows it on the article: Der Salat ist gut (subject), but Ich esse den Salat (object).

pattern: ich möchte + object · ich möchte + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: möchte means 'would like'. It is the polite way to ask for things in a café or shop: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte. ich and er/sie/es have the same form, möchte, with no -t. With a second verb, that verb goes to the end in the infinitive: Ich möchte bezahlen.
compare_en: Like 'would like', möchte is more polite than 'want'. But there is no 'to' before the second verb: Ich möchte bezahlen = I would like to pay.

pattern: kein + noun · nicht + verb, adjective or der/die/das/mein + noun
explain: Use kein for 'no' or 'not a' before a noun that would have ein or no article: Ich habe keinen Hund. Ich trinke keinen Kaffee. kein takes the same endings as ein, and keine in the plural. Use nicht for everything else: verbs, adjectives, and nouns with der/die/das or mein: Das Essen ist nicht gut. Das ist nicht mein Tee.
compare_en: English says 'not a', 'not any' or 'no': I don't have a dog. German simply uses kein: Ich habe keinen Hund. Never say nicht ein.

pattern: der Tisch → die Tische · die Tür → die Türen · das Bild → die Bilder · das Sofa → die Sofas
explain: German has several plural endings, so learn each noun with its plural: der Tisch, die Tische. The plural article is always die. Rough guide: most feminine nouns add -(e)n; many masculine nouns add -e, sometimes with an umlaut (ä, ö, ü); short neuter nouns often add -er with an umlaut; words from other languages add -s; nouns ending in -er often stay the same.
compare_en: English nearly always adds -s (tables, rooms). In German -s is the rarest ending, mostly for borrowed words like Sofas and Fotos. Some nouns don't change at all, like 'sheep': das Zimmer → die Zimmer.

pattern: Es gibt + accusative (einen / eine / ein / –)
explain: es gibt means 'there is' or 'there are'. It never changes: es gibt for one thing and for many things. What follows is an object (accusative), so masculine nouns take einen or keinen: Es gibt einen Balkon. In a question the verb comes first: Gibt es hier einen Aufzug?
compare_en: English switches between 'there is' and 'there are'. German always says es gibt (literally 'it gives'), followed by the accusative.

pattern: noun + sein + adjective (no ending)
explain: An adjective describes something: groß (big), klein (small), hell (bright), ruhig (quiet), teuer (expensive). After sein the adjective has no ending at all, whatever the gender or number: Der Balkon ist klein. Die Küche ist klein. Die Zimmer sind klein. You can add sehr (very), zu (too) or nicht (not) in front of it.
compare_en: Just like English: The room is big. The adjective only gets an ending when it stands before a noun (ein großes Zimmer), which you will learn later.

pattern: subject + VERB (position 2) + … + PREFIX (at the end)
explain: Some verbs have a small front part, the prefix: auf-, an-, ein-, mit-, fern-. In a normal sentence the prefix splits off and goes to the very end: aufstehen → Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf. The main part stands in position 2 as usual. In the dictionary the verb is one word, and the prefix is stressed: AUFstehen.
compare_en: English has verbs like this too: get up, call up, come along. German just pushes the small part to the end of the sentence, even after a long middle: Ich rufe morgen um acht Uhr Lena an.

pattern: um + clock time · am + day / part of the day · im + month / season · von … bis …
explain: Use um for clock times (um 8 Uhr), am for days and parts of the day (am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende), and im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Winter). von … bis means 'from … to/until': von 9 bis 17 Uhr. One exception: in der Nacht (at night).
compare_en: English uses at, on and in (at 8, on Monday, in May), and German uses um, am and im the same way. But 'in the evening' is am Abend, and 'at the weekend' is am Wochenende.

pattern: Time / place + VERB + subject + rest
explain: You can start a sentence with a time (heute, am Montag, um 8 Uhr) instead of the subject. The verb must still stand in position 2, so the subject moves behind the verb: Ich arbeite am Montag → Am Montag arbeite ich. This is very common in German.
compare_en: English keeps the subject before the verb: On Monday I work. In German that order is wrong (Am Montag ich arbeite ✗). The verb stays second, and the subject comes third.

pattern: only du and er / sie / es: a → ä · e → i · e → ie
explain: Some common verbs change their vowel, but only with du and er/sie/es: fahren → du fährst, er fährt; sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; lesen → du liest, sie liest. All other forms are regular: ich fahre, wir fahren, ihr fahrt. Learn these verbs together with their er form.
compare_en: English has nothing like this in the present tense. A tip: if the er form changes, the du form changes in the same way, and the rest stays regular.

pattern: verb + gern · verb + lieber · verb + am liebsten
explain: To say you like doing something, put gern after the verb: Ich tanze gern (I like dancing). lieber means 'prefer' and am liebsten means 'like best of all': Ich schwimme lieber. Am liebsten lese ich. nicht gern means 'don't like'. For things you like, use mögen instead: Ich mag Kaffee.
compare_en: English uses the verb 'like': I like swimming. German keeps the action verb and adds the little word gern: Ich schwimme gern, literally 'I swim gladly'.

pattern: subject + kann / will (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: können (can, be able to) and wollen (want to) are modal verbs. The modal verb stands in position 2, and the main verb goes to the very end in the infinitive: Ich kann gut schwimmen. Lena will ins Kino gehen. ich and er/sie/es have the same form with no ending: ich kann, er kann; ich will, sie will.
compare_en: German will means 'want to', not 'will': Ich will tanzen = I want to dance. And English keeps the two verbs together (I can swim well), while German splits them: Ich kann gut schwimmen.

pattern: ich → mich · du → dich · er → ihn · sie → sie · es → es · wir → uns · ihr → euch
explain: When a pronoun is the object (the person or thing the action is done to), some forms change: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, ihr → euch. sie, es and Sie stay the same. For things, the pronoun follows the gender: der Computer → ihn, die Jacke → sie, das Handy → es.
compare_en: English does this for people: he → him, we → us. German does it for things too: die Jacke is sie, so 'I'll take it' is Ich nehme sie.

pattern: subject + verb + meinen / deinen / seinen / ihren + masculine noun
explain: Possessives (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr) take the same endings as ein. So as an object, only masculine nouns change: mein → meinen. Ich suche meinen Schlüssel. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same: meine Tasche, mein Handy, meine Schuhe.
compare_en: English 'my' never changes. In German the ending shows whether the noun is the subject or the object: Mein Schlüssel ist weg (subject), Ich suche meinen Schlüssel (object).

pattern: welcher / welche / welches …? – dieser / diese / dieses
explain: welch- asks 'which?' when you choose between things, and dies- means 'this' and points at one. Both take endings like der, die, das: der → -er, die → -e, das → -es, plural die → -e. As an object, masculine -er becomes -en, just like der → den: Welchen Computer kaufst du? – Diesen.
compare_en: English 'which' and 'this' never change. In German the ending matches the article: der Schuh → dieser Schuh, die Jacke → diese Jacke, das Handy → dieses Handy.

pattern: Sie: Gehen Sie …! · du: Geh …! · ihr: Geht …!
explain: The imperative gives instructions, directions and requests, and the verb comes first. Sie: the verb + Sie (Gehen Sie geradeaus!). du: take the du form and drop du and -st (du kommst → Komm!). ihr: the ihr form without ihr (ihr kommt → Kommt!). The change e → i stays (Nimm!), but a → ä does not (Fahr!). Add bitte to sound polite.
compare_en: English has one form for everyone: Go straight on! German has three, depending on who you are talking to, and the Sie form keeps its pronoun: Gehen Sie!

pattern: mit / zu / von / aus / bei / nach + dative: dem · der · dem · den
explain: After mit, zu, von, aus, bei and nach the noun is always in the dative case. The articles change: der → dem, das → dem, die → der, plural die → den. Short forms: zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, von dem → vom, bei dem → beim. Use nach for towns and countries (nach Berlin), but zu for people and places (zum Arzt, zur Post).
compare_en: English 'to' can be zu or nach: nach Berlin, but zum Bahnhof and zu Lena. And after mit the article always changes: mit dem Bus (by bus).

pattern: Wo? (place) · Woher? (from where) · Wohin? (to where)
explain: German has three question words for places. wo? asks where something is: Wo ist die Post? woher? asks where from: Woher kommst du? – Aus Indien. wohin? asks where to: Wohin fährst du? – Nach Köln. Verbs of movement like gehen and fahren go with wohin; sein and wohnen go with wo.
compare_en: English uses 'where' for all three. A tip: if the English question could end in 'to' or 'from' (Where are you going to? Where are you from?), use wohin or woher.

pattern: subject + muss (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: müssen means 'must' or 'have to': something is necessary. Like all modal verbs it stands in position 2, and the main verb goes to the end in the infinitive: Ich muss zum Arzt gehen. ich and er/sie/es both say muss, with no ending. Careful: nicht müssen means 'don't have to': Du musst nicht kommen.
compare_en: English 'must not' means it is forbidden, but German muss nicht only means 'not necessary'. For 'must not', German uses darf nicht.

pattern: subject + darf (position 2) + … + infinitive (at the end)
explain: dürfen means 'may' or 'be allowed to'. Use it to ask for permission or to give it: Darf ich hier sitzen? With nicht it means 'must not', so it is forbidden: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. ich and er/sie/es have no ending, and the singular has no umlaut: ich darf, er darf.
compare_en: Darf ich …? is like 'May I …?'. And darf nicht is English 'must not' (not allowed), while muss nicht only means 'don't have to'.

pattern: position 1 + MODAL (position 2) + … middle … + INFINITIVE (end)
explain: With a modal verb (können, müssen, dürfen, wollen, möchten) a German sentence makes a frame, the verb bracket: the modal verb in position 2 and the infinitive at the very end. Everything else (time, object, place, nicht) goes in the middle. A separable verb stays in one piece at the end: Ich muss früh aufstehen.
compare_en: In English the two verbs stand together: I must take a tablet. In German they open and close the sentence like a bracket: Ich muss eine Tablette nehmen.

pattern: subject + haben (position 2) + … + Partizip II (end): ge- + stem + -t
explain: The Perfekt is the usual way to talk about the past when you speak or write a message. It has two parts: haben in position 2 and the Partizip II (past participle) at the end. For regular verbs the participle is ge- + stem + -t: kaufen → gekauft, arbeiten → gearbeitet. Verbs ending in -ieren have no ge-: studieren → studiert.
compare_en: English often uses the simple past (I bought a ticket yesterday), but German says Ich habe gestern ein Ticket gekauft, literally 'I have bought'. And the participle goes to the end, not next to haben.

pattern: subject + sein (position 2) + … + Partizip II (end)
explain: Some verbs use sein instead of haben in the Perfekt. These are verbs of movement from one place to another (fahren, fliegen, gehen, kommen, reisen), a few verbs of change (aufstehen), and sein and bleiben themselves: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. Wir sind zu Hause geblieben. All other verbs take haben.
compare_en: English always uses 'have' (I have gone), so this is new. Think 'movement from A to B = sein': Ich bin geflogen (I flew), but Ich habe ein Ticket gebucht (I booked a ticket).

pattern: ge- + stem (often with a new vowel) + -en
explain: Many common verbs are irregular: their Partizip II ends in -en, and the vowel often changes: trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben, finden → gefunden. Some keep their vowel: essen → gegessen, sehen → gesehen. There is no rule to guess them, so learn each verb with its participle.
compare_en: English has irregular verbs too, and some look alike: drink – drunk, trinken – getrunken; find – found, finden – gefunden.

pattern: am + ordinal + -en (am ersten Mai) · im + month (im Juli)
explain: Dates use ordinal numbers (first, second …). Up to 19 add -te (zweite, vierte), from 20 add -ste (zwanzigste); erste, dritte, siebte and achte are special. 'On' a date is am + ordinal + -en: am ersten Mai. In writing a dot shows the ordinal: am 3. Oktober (say am dritten). For a whole month use im: im Juli.
compare_en: English writes 1st, 2nd, 3rd; German writes 1., 2., 3. and says am ersten, am zweiten, am dritten. 'In July' is im Juli, and 'today is the first' is Heute ist der erste.

pattern: Es + weather verb (Es regnet.) · Es ist + adjective (Es ist kalt.)
explain: For the weather German always uses es as the subject, like English 'it': Es regnet (it's raining). Es ist kalt. Es ist warm. Because es is the subject, the verb takes the er/sie/es form. In a question or after a time phrase, es comes right after the verb: Regnet es? Im Winter ist es kalt.
compare_en: Like English 'it is raining', but German has no -ing: Es regnet means both 'it rains' and 'it's raining'. Never drop es: Heute ist kalt ✗ → Heute ist es kalt ✓.

pattern: prefix + ge + participle: einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen
explain: In the Perfekt of a separable verb, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, einladen → eingeladen. The participle is one word, at the end. Movement and change verbs still take sein: Ich bin um 7 Uhr aufgestanden. Der Zug ist pünktlich angekommen.
compare_en: English keeps the small word separate (I called him up). German glues it to the front of the participle, with ge- in the middle: Ich habe ihn angerufen.
